steps: This flow is about access control at retrieval. A billing clerk asks the assistant which procedure codes were billed for patient P one two three four five.
First, the wrong way. A shared service token pulls every match, diagnoses included, straight into the prompt, and the system prompt is told to hide the clinical parts. By then it is already too late.
Now the right way. Your design passes the clerk's own identity, billing clerk forty-seven, never a shared token, and that identity carries only billing and demographics roles.
Retrieval applies the access control filter inside the vector database query, matching allowed roles to the user's roles. Only billing passages come back, and diagnosis data never leaves the index.
Next, only the authorized passages reach prompt construction, which can simply trust retrieval, because the access rule is already enforced there.
Claude answers the clerk from those passages only, citing a source I D for each claim, so the answer is grounded and checkable.

Finally, your answer to compliance: restricted documents never leave the retrieval layer. It is deterministic, not a prompt promise, and the audit shows exactly which documents clerk forty-seven received.
